source.title: The case for 4-bit precision: k-bit Inference Scaling Laws

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study reports scaling results in a new setting: zero-shot inference with quantized language-model weights. It measures downstream-task accuracy across model sizes and bit precisions, and evaluates whether power functions fit those inference results.
record.gate_note: The paper does not test pretraining cross-entropy scaling with parameters, tokens, or training compute, nor compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. Its CommonCrawl cross-entropy results concern quantized inference and are not the pretraining-scaling measure in V1–V3. The rows below concern downstream zero-shot accuracy (V6) and the study's explicit finding about power-function fit (V7).
record.test_reason: The study borrows the scaling-law framing to compare quantization bit precisions at a fixed total model-bit budget during zero-shot inference. Its results concern quantized pretrained checkpoints: which precision is bit-optimal, and which quantization methods improve that trade-off. It does not measure pretraining loss against parameters, tokens or compute, compute-optimal allocation, architecture shape, or whether downstream accuracy is predictable from scale or pretraining loss. Accuracy rising with total model bits is a by-product of evaluating existing checkpoints, not a test of downstream predictability. The reported poor fit of bivariate power functions concerns accuracy as a function of parameters and bit precision at inference. It is not about training-law exponents or how fitting choices shift them. These are related but different constructs, so they are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude 4-bit precision is almost universally optimal for total model bits versus zero-shot accuracy, across the families and scales tested. Small block sizes and float or quantile data types are the only methods that improve bit-level scaling, and nothing helps at 6–8 bits. Outlier-dependent (proxy) quantization stabilises 3-bit OPT and Pythia but does not beat 4-bit. One-shot methods such as GPTQ look promising below 4 bits.
record.recipe_differences: This is an inference-time quantization study measuring zero-shot accuracy and perplexity across model-bit budgets and quantization precisions, rather than a training scaling-law study of held-out loss versus parameters, tokens, and compute.
record.method_sensitivity: Bit precision changes the outcome; 3-bit is unstable for OPT and Pythia, while BLOOM and GPT-2 remain stable. Block size and quantization data type also change accuracy in the study's additional experiments.

fits_no_version.finding: Across 19M–176B models in five families, 4-bit precision maximises mean zero-shot accuracy for a fixed total model-bit budget. Lowering precision from 16 to 4 bits helps; at 3 bits performance degrades, and OPT and Pythia become near-random at large sizes.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Bit-level inference scaling: for a fixed memory budget, 4-bit quantized larger models beat higher-precision smaller models.

fits_no_version.finding: Bivariate power functions of parameter count and bit precision fit the inference accuracy data poorly. Linear interpolations show near-parallel curves across precisions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Quantized-inference accuracy scaling is not well described by a joint power law in parameters and bit precision.

fits_no_version.finding: Across more than 35,000 quantized-inference experiments, Pile-CC perplexity and mean zero-shot accuracy correlate with Pearson r = -0.94.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under quantization perturbations, held-out perplexity tracks zero-shot accuracy closely.

record.problems: The paper says zero-shot accuracy is noisier than perplexity. Most curve values are shown in figures rather than tabulated, and uncertainty estimates are not stated for these results. The reported poor power-function fit is qualitative and concerns inference quantization, not training-loss scaling.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for 5–16-bit curves, quantization data types, block sizes, or the Appendix C.5 CommonCrawl cross-entropy plots. Those results concern quantization-method comparisons or inference perplexity rather than the tested downstream-accuracy and fit claims recorded here; the main paper and Appendices C.1–C.5 contain them.

untested.parts: Pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute; no training runs.
Extrapolating fitted laws to larger training runs.
Architecture shape at fixed parameter count.
Other modalities or training regimes; quantized inference is not a training regime.
Predictability of downstream accuracy from scale or pretraining loss; accuracy is only plotted as a function of total model bits under quantization.
Dependence of training-law exponents or compute-optimal split on setup and fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V6 and V7 links conflate inference-time precision trade-offs with the scaling-law claims about training. The Appendix C.5 CC-Pile cross-entropy curves are loss of quantized checkpoints against total bits, not pretraining loss scaling, so they bear on no version either. No verdicts are given.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
Predicting much larger runs from power laws fitted on smaller training runs.
Compute-optimal allocation between model parameters and training tokens.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Other modalities and training regimes such as repeated data, fine-tuning, and transfer; the study concerns text-model quantization at inference.
The study measures zero-shot accuracy across quantized model-size/bit settings, but does not fit or validate a predictor of downstream performance from pretraining loss or scale.
It reports a poor fit for bivariate power functions in its inference setting, but does not test how training-law exponents or compute-optimal allocation vary with training setup.
